Reinsurer TIG found liable over Libby Mine asbestos exposure claims

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Courthousenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Omaha-based National Indemnity sued, saying the reinsurer did not fully cover its losses after Montana failed to warn of the dangers in and around the small city of Libby.
  • It has been revealed that OMAHA, Neb.
  • Jurors found National Indemnity complied with its obligations under the reinsurance certificate and proved its breach of contract claim against TIG.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Omaha-based National Indemnity sued, saying the reinsurer did not fully cover its losses after Montana failed to warn of the dangers in and around the small city of Libby.

It has been revealed that OMAHA, Neb. (CN) â An eight-person federal jury found reinsurer TIG liable after Omaha-based National Indemnity claimed TIG didn’t fully cover a sweeping payout for widespread asbestos contamination from the Libby Mine.

Jurors found National Indemnity complied with its obligations under the reinsurance certificate and proved its breach of contract claim against TIG. They awarded National Indemnity $39.2 million in indemnity, $3.2 million in prejudgment interest, $21.1 million in postjudgment interest and $16.1 million in expenses.

They declined to award National Indemnity any future defense costs.

Attorneys for both sides declined to comment after the verdict was read.

National Indemnity Insurance Company turned to TIG Insurance Company and other reinsurers after agreeing in 2022, with Montana, to resolve all coverage claims over asbestos exposure from the mine since the 1960s for $157 million.

National Indemnity insured the state from July 1, 1973, to July 1, 1975; TIG provided the firm’s reinsurance at that time.

TIG claimed National Indemnity did not offer adequate evidence and billed amounts not covered by the reinsurance agreement, essentially finagling the numbers to make TIG cover part of the massive bill.

Sources indicate that âIt lied," said Scott L. Davis, a Dallas-based attorney for the Spencer Fane firm, representing TIG, speaking of National Indemnity during closing arguments late Thursday afternoon.

National Indemnity said it kept TIG informed throughout the claims process, but the reinsurer never got involved, something it had a right to do.

“They could have helped; they didnât,” Michael Knoerzer, a Upcoming York-based attorney for Clyde & Co., representing National Indemnity, told the jury Thursday. âItâs undisputed in this case they never asked.â.

In 2004, the state of Montana was found liable for asbestos risk to miners and residents near Libby, a small city in the state’s northwest.

Recent findings suggest that from 1963 to 1990, W.R. Grace & Co. extracted vermiculite at the mine, about 7 miles outside of Libby. Vermiculite, once commonly used for fireproof roofing, insulation and wallpaper, is not dangerous. But the asbestos the mining stirred up was.

Decades of widespread asbestos contamination from the mine caused the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to declare its first-ever public health emergency during a 2009 Superfund cleanup.

Sources indicate that thousands of W.R. Grace workers, their families and residents since the 1960s have been injured or died from lung disease related to working at or living near the mine.

Recent findings suggest that the fight over who should be held liable started about 2000, shortly after reports of workers falling ill sparked an emergency cleanup. Contamination has since been blamed for hundreds of deaths.

Reinsurance is dubbed âinsurance for insurance companiesâ by the Reinsurance Association of America. Under reinsurance, one insurance tech giant indemnifies another for a loss the company buying the policy cannot handle alone â something that National Indemnity claims TIG did not fully do.

Industry observers note that after the $157 million payout, National Indemnity billed its reinsurers more than $101 million. They did not pay. Since first filing the lawsuit in 2022, all other reinsurers except TIG have been dropped from the suit. TIG has paid National Indemnity what it believed it owed â $12.7 million.

It has been revealed that according to National Indemnity, the insurance contract required National Indemnity to pay as much as $3 million per loss, with unlimited occurrences. At first, the state said 21 occurrences involved state inspectors not warning miners about the asbestos risk.

But National Indemnity feared that, with potentially thousands of miners and locals affected by asbestos exposure, the number of occurrences could multiply as the matter moved again through Montana courts, with the state Supreme Court telling the parties to litigate the number of occurrences.

Ultimately, National Indemnity and the state settled at 27 occurrences. At $3 million apiece, the bill came to $81 million. The roughly $76 million remaining largely came from past and present defense costs.

Under their contract, TIG was responsible for one-third of National Indemnityâs costs. So, according to National Indemnity, it would have to pay $1 million for each occurrence.

Industry observers note that montana and National Indemnity counted each failure to warn by the state as an occurrence. At issue is whether individual deaths could also count as an occurrence. National Indemnity argued it could have found itself on the hook for âbillionsâ if individual deaths were counted, which led it to settle at 27.

In her instructions to the jury Thursday, U.S. District Judge Susan M. Bazis said National Indemnity would have to prove, by greater weight of evidence, that it performed its obligation under the contract and that TIG breached it, causing damages to the Omaha-based insurer.

According to recent reports, the Joe Biden appointee said TIG agreed there was adequate proof of 21 occurrences. National Indemnity would have to prove it provided satisfactory evidence of each occurrence to TIG.

Industry observers note that “By greater weight of the evidence” is a less strict standard than the “beyond a reasonable doubt” standard in criminal cases. As in criminal cases, the jury selects a foreperson, and the vote must be unanimous.

Build on the strength of the RevOps team: prioritize its roadmap against business outcomes and take on more strategic work together.

Launch your first AI-enabled workflows or automations that remove manual reporting or reconciliation for the commercial teams, with time saved tracked.

Have a team whose output and standards hold, with the processes, tooling, and automation you've built running without you in the room.

Have AI-enabled, self-serve tooling that commercial teams use day to day, with measurable time savings.

Be the person leadership trusts to pick up the next important thing that doesn't have an owner yet.

A clear communicator who can walk an executive through a messy problem and leave them with a decision, and who is just as effective working alongside an AE, a CSM, or an engineer.

Trump administration withdraws application to Supreme Court to block lower court ruling on protected status for Venezuelan nationals

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18; updated with latest developments on Nov.
  • The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon.
  • Recent findings suggest that then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Originally published on Nov. 18; updated with latest developments on Nov. 19 at 4:35 p.m.

The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”.

Recent findings suggest that then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he revealed that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

After Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, announced her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

Industry observers note that in June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled – in a pair of cases involving Haitian and Syrian TPS beneficiaries – that courts generally cannot review the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to designate or terminate a country under the TPS program. Relying on that decision, the Trump administration asked the court to send the Venezuelan TPS case back to the 9th Circuit for another look, which the court did in October of this year.

When the case returned to the 9th Circuit, Sauer told the justices, and the Supreme Court’s initial stay of Chen’s ruling expired, the court of appeals entered an administrative stay, which is due to expire on Nov. 20. “Absent judicial intervention between now and” then, Sauer wrote, “the Department of Homeland Security will have to resurrect TPS status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans after a nineteen-month hiatus.” Indeed, he noted, his office “has been informed that the government could be forced to immediately release into the country some 1800 or so Venezuelan aliens from detention.” And all of this would result, he continued, even though the Supreme Court has already “conclusively held in Doe” that the TPS statute bars courts from reviewing the DHS secretary’s decision to designate or end the designation of TPS.

Industry observers note that on Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its application. In a letter to Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, Sauer explained that “a few hours after we filed our stay application, the court of appeals issued an order” extending its current administrative stay (and therefore keeping Chen’s ruling on hold) until seven days after it challenges a decision. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” Sauer added, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After adding cases on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border and the standard for securities-fraud lawsuits to the oral argument docket last Friday, the justices began this week by denying a number of notable petitions, including two DEI-related disputes. Then, on Wednesday, the Trump administration brought a familiar battle back to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the court to address its effort to remove protected status from Venezuelan nationals. The administration withdrew that request on Thursday, however, citing a fresh lower-court ruling.

Finally, a few housekeeping notes:.

According to recent reports, on Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from Thomas Overton, who was sentenced to death for killing Michael and Susan “Missy” MacIvor and their unborn child in 1991. Hours later, Overton was executed in Florida.

It has been revealed that also on Thursday, the court denied a request for a stay of execution from Reinaldo Dennes, who was sentenced to death for the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs. Hours later, Dennes was executed in Texas.

On Wednesday, the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work when they cannot return home – returned to the Supreme Court, as the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 district court ruling that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. As noted above, the government withdrew that request on Thursday.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, December 4. The disputes address such challenges as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and its approach to appointing acting U.S. attorneys.

The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in dozens of cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.

The Supreme Court Building will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, November 26, and Friday, November 27.

Recent findings suggest that the December argument session will begin on Monday, November 30. On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of AR-15 bans, at 10:00 a.m. EST. We will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

Michael Phillis, Associated Press.

In a petition for review filed earlier this month, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on “its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever,” according to the Associated Press. “Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels,” but after President Donald Trump took office, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the grants. Groups that lost the money challenged this decision, and “[i]n August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and said the administration improperly terminated the grants.” “The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups.”.

On Thursday, U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday “allowed President Donald Trump to proceed with portions of his $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and Penguin Random House LLC,” in which the president accuses the news outlet and publisher “of tarnishing his reputation with false stories about his business acumen before the 2024 presidential election,” according to Bloomberg. Merryday concluded that “Trump had sufficiently alleged ‘actual malice’ in connection with” seven “disputed statements, which requires showing that the authors and publishers knew the statements were false or recklessly disregarded whether they were false. It’s a high bar that must be met by public figures who sue for defamation, established by the Supreme Court decades ago to protect press freedoms.”.

Nicholas Kristof, The Newly introduced York Times.

According to recent reports, in a column for The Upcoming York Times, Nicholas Kristof described meeting with five men who were deported from the United States to South Sudan through a process known as “third-country removals” that has been embraced by the Trump administration and will soon be considered by the Supreme Court. The men, according to Kristof, “were nearly starving, can’t regularly communicate with their families or anyone else and don’t have any path to get to their home countries or, in the case of some of them, to ever see their American citizen children again.” “I hope the justices will take note of what has happened to those sent to South Sudan,” he wrote.

In a recent development, in a post for his Substack, Ed Whelan reflected on the potential reasons why Judge Cornelia Kennedy of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit, who was once described by a senator as “probably the most exceptional woman judge in the country,” was passed over for a Supreme Court nomination in favor of “a virtual unknown, Sandra Day O’Connor,” amid President Ronald Reagans quest “to nominate the first female justice.” O’Connor likely benefitted from, among other things, having “a powerful advocate” in Chief Justice Warren Burger, who “energetically lobb[ied] for O’Connor with White House officials and evidently with Reagan himself.” A comparison between O’Connor and Kennedy “offers lessons about the pressures and incentives that shape a president’s selection of a Supreme Court nominee,” Whelan wrote.

According to recent reports, in a piece on the legacy of Judge Richard Posner, who died on November 10, The Economist celebrated his remarkable career, describing him as “a giant of American law.” Scholars told the publication that “Posner may prove more influential than many Supreme Court justices,” in large part because he wrote “more than 500 articles, 50 books and 3,300 judicial opinions on everything from the law and sex to how judges think” during his career. “We pay attention to the justices because their opinions matter, but very few of them have anything interesting or original to offer,” noted Larry Kramer of the London School of Economics. “Dick Posner did.”.

On Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its request for the Supreme Court to block a lower court ruling that would allow Venezuelan nationals to participate in the Temporary Protected Status program, noting that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit has ensured the ruling will remain on hold. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” wrote U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”.

Time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Despite being short on time, however, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.

Sources indicate that the Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Levi Woodbury, who served on the court from 1845 to 1851.

Being the first justice to attend law school and the first of two New Hampshire justices (the second being Justice David Souter) has not saved Justice Levi Woodbury’s reputation from “declin[ing] dramatically over the years,” as a “reputational study” of the justice published in the Journal of Supreme Court History put it.

Woodbury was born in December 1789 in Francestown, Latest Hampshire. As the eldest son, he faced immense pressure to succeed and was “near obsessive” about his education, according to Oyez. He attended Atkinson Academy before enrolling at Dartmouth at 16, earning money teaching in the towns around Hanover to afford school.

According to recent reports, woodbury then attended law school (the other justices had “read law” through apprenticeships or were self-taught), studying at Litchfield Law school in Connecticut. Per Oyez, however, his time there was brief: He promptly came to the conclusion that he “did not enjoy [law school]” and apprenticed instead before being admitted to the bar in 1812.

During the War of 1812, Woodbury drafted the Hillsborough Resolves, statements backing President James Madison’s decision to fight Britain (and arguing against Daniel Webster’s condemnation of the war). With this, Woodbury became “one of the few” Fresh Englanders to support the War of 1812. While then clerking for the state Senate, Woodbury connected with Gov. William Plumer, who in 1816 appointed Woodbury, then 27, to the New Hampshire Superior Court (the state’s top court).

Industry observers note that in 1823, the Fresh Hampshire Democratic-Republicans faced “bitter factionalism within,” and a group of them (displeased with their caucus’ choice for governor) chose Woodbury as their nominee instead, helping him to become New Hampshire’s 15th governor by a significant margin. Woodbury’s attempt to reunite the party met with little success, however, and he was not reelected. Still, by 1825 Woodbury had become speaker of the state House and a U.S. senator and later chaired the Senate Committee on Commerce. During that time, Woodbury, who was sympathetic to President Andrew Jackson, supported the Indian Removal Act of 1830. He was subsequently appointed by Jackson in March 1831 as secretary of the Navy.

In 1834, Jackson shifted Woodbury to the Treasury, where he denied entrusting federal money to the Second Bank of the United States (like his predecessor, Roger B. Taney), instead giving it to commercial banks. In that position, he also issued the Specie Circular, which directed federal land offices to accept “nothing except what is directed by the existing laws, viz, gold and silver, and in the proper cases Virginia land scrip,” but not paper money, for land purchases. The Circular is often cited as a “primary cause” of the Panic of 1837.

In 1841, Woodbury returned to the Senate rather than serve as chief justice of Fresh Hampshire’s Superior Court. After Justice Joseph Story died in September 1845, President James Polk nominated Woodbury as a recess appointment to the Supreme Court, and he was confirmed by the Senate that January.

Industry observers note that in 1847, Woodbury authored the court’s unanimous opinion in Jones v. Van Zandt, which upheld the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 as constitutional. Oyez writes that although “[m]any thought this indicated a pro-slavery stance … really his vote was motivated by an appreciation for states’ rights and a fear that the constitution was being interpreted too liberally.” Yet whereas Justice John McLean wrote that “the Constitution treats slaves as persons,” Woodbury “repeatedly referr[ed] to enslaved people as ‘property.’” One anti-slavery paper wrote that “if there be a man in the United States utterly heartless on the subject of slavery, it is Levi Woodbury” and that “[w]e know of no opinion on record of any slaveholding court, so inhumane in tone and language, as the opinion of Judge Woodbury, declared in the Van Zandt case.”.

Sources indicate that in 1849’s Luther v. Borden, Woodbury was the only justice to dissent, concluding that Rhode Island’s statute establishing martial law was unconstitutional. Under such a law, he wrote, the “whole population” was “exposed … to be seized, without warrant or oath” and that “[b]y it, every citizen … exists with, a rope around his neck.” Woodbury likewise dissented in 1849’s Passenger Cases, which asked whether a tax could be imposed “upon alien passengers” arriving in the ports of New York and Massachusetts. Woodbury wrote that the commerce clause did not give the federal government exclusive immigration powers, and that states could tax immigrants after they arrived in the state ports.

Woodbury also pursued his political ambitions while on the court. In 1848, John C. Calhoun said – reportedly influenced by Woodbury’s decision in Van Zandt – that he “would run best in the South.” Woodbury campaigned for president, but his apparent efforts to appeal to both slavery and anti-slavery advocates hurt his candidacy, and Lewis Cass ultimately received the Democratic nomination.

Although Woodbury “looked like a front-runner again for an 1852 nomination,” he died in 1851 in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, at age 61, and the nomination went to his former clerk, Franklin Pierce.

MR. MILLER: “– No, I think they mean what a district judge honoring his Article III commission concludes after an intensive evaluation of the entirety of the complaint, looking for that strong inference, putting on his sort of motion to dismiss 12(b)(6) hat, says okay –”.

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: “Just okay?”.

Sources indicate that MR. MILLER: “– No, I did not mean that. Don't take me literally on that. For heavens sakes, I'm from Brooklyn. I'm very colloquial. I'm very sorry about that.”.

JUSTICE SCALIA: “Let me write that down. We should not take you literally. All right.”.

— Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Complications & Rights, Ltd. (2007).

    • Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

    Industry observers note that but the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a fresh estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”.

    Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    #67030. Industry News: Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2333 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite.
    • Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.
    • Sources indicate that every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

    Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.

    Sources indicate that every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

    “[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

    Industry observers note that but why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”.

    Sources indicate that thus, a fundamental premise of criminal law, Winship, is constitutional law too. Moreover, and just by the way, Winship demonstrates that the “incorporation” theory of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause (that is, applying the Bill of Rights to the states) is not limited to concepts stated expressly in the Bill of Rights itself – as “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” is not. Critics of non-textual constitutional rights – like privacy, a right to travel, a right to refuse medical treatment (like mask wearing?), or even a right to terminate a pregnancy – must confront the application of their literalist theory to proof beyond a reasonable doubt, too. For this reason, I also teach Winship in every constitutional law class.

    There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution.

    This sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

    So the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.).

    Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure.

    Recent findings suggest that three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

    According to recent reports, one example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

    Sources indicate that why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

    In a recent development, (Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.).

    Industry observers note that in addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

    And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution.

    In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then Upcoming York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

    Criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

    Sources indicate that in addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it claims,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

    For example, Griswold v. Connecticut recognized a constitutional right to privacy in the criminal law context, resting in part (and almost entirely for three justices) on the Ninth Amendment. Less controversially, perhaps, Chief Justice Warren Burger later invoked the amendment in the 1980 case of Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia to support an “unarticulated” constitutional right for the public (and the press) to attend criminal trials. And in 2000, even Justice Antonin Scalia agreed (in a solo dissent to Troxel v. Granville, a non-criminal case) that the Ninth Amendment recognizes unenumerated rights. When you tell your Thanksgiving dinner companions that criminal law is constitutional law, don’t forget the Ninth Amendment.

    So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law.

    Industry observers note that thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

    Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law.

    By now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

    Just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

    In a recent development, immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory concerns in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

    In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

    Last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, massive and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

    Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

    Recommended Citation: Rory Little, Criminal law is constitutional law, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/criminal-law-is-constitutional-law/.

    • think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    Our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end owners, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk. We are hiring a Security Engineer to build and run our vulnerability management and security operations program. Vulnerability management is a core capability for keeping our security posture strong as the platform and the tech giant grow: knowing what we run, finding what is exposed, and getting the right fixes shipped quickly. It also underpins our customer commitments and the compliance programs we are building. Our program is early, and you will shape it. You will join a small Trust team that covers security, IT and compliance, and you will own this program end to end from your first week.

    think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.

    take an automation-first and pragmatic approach to risk mitigation.

    translate security concerns into engineering action.

    can clearly explain complex technical concepts to others.

    are a fast learner and thrive in ambiguity.

    Select, deploy and operationalize scanning tooling across our production assets.

    Run vulnerability management end to end: triage, severity in our environment, owner assignment, remediation SLAs and reporting.

    Build engineering-first triage and remediation workflows that fit how our engineering teams already work, and automate the routing and follow-up.

    Build a remediation dashboard that engineering and leadership read and act on.

    Automate collection of the vulnerability management evidence our compliance programs depend on, in partnership with our Compliance team.

    Build automation, including agentic tooling, that removes manual security operations work and keeps pace with engineering growth.

    5+ years in security engineering, security operations or software engineering, with a significant share of that focused on security.

    Hands-on experience building or running a vulnerability management program or software security tooling (SCA, container, cloud or host scanning).

    An engineering-first approach to triage and remediation: you get findings fixed by making the fix easy to ship.

    The judgment to set a finding's real severity in our environment, using CVSS as one input.

    Strong scripting and automation skills in a language such as Go or Python, and comfort reading infrastructure as code such as Terraform.

    A pragmatic approach to risk: you can explain why a finding matters to the business and how fast it needs to be fixed.

    Experience with real-time media, networking or WebRTC systems.

    Experience supporting compliance audits such as HIPAA, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001 or SOC 2.

    Incident response or application security experience.

    Experience in AI security, such as securing LLM applications or agent infrastructure.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    LiveKit is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate on the basis of any characteristic protected by applicable law. If you require a reasonable accommodation during the application or interview process, please contact recruiting@livekit.io.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Social media advertising continues to grow, but not all ads are created equal.
    • DoubleVerify compiled its report by collecting responses from 22,000 consumers and 2,020 marketers, spanning regions like North America, Latin America, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific.
    • Those users are also warming up to YouTube’s ad ecosystem.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Social media advertising continues to grow, but not all ads are created equal. The ad tech company DoubleVerify has released its 2026 Global Insights Report, a dispatch that identifies YouTube and Facebook — and their respective short-form formats — as dominant forces in the social media marketing landscape.

    DoubleVerify compiled its report by collecting responses from 22,000 consumers and 2,020 marketers, spanning regions like North America, Latin America, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific. One thing those global respondents can agree on is their appreciation of YouTube. Google’s video hub is the most-used platform across all age groups and regions, with 95% of all respondents claiming to use it.

    Those users are also warming up to YouTube’s ad ecosystem. Half of the respondents mentioned they would take action based on YouTube ads; that was the highest percentage among all measured platforms. Facebook came in second on that axis (49%), followed by Instagram (42%) and TikTok (38%).

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    In a recent development, other platforms are lagging behind in terms of actionable ads, and DoubleVerify’s findings suggest a big difference between those four industry leaders and their competitors. YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok are four platforms where short-form media has been widely adopted, and 38% of DoubleVerify respondents said that short-form ads inspire them to take action. That was 7% higher than the next ad format on the list (long-form video pre-rolls, at 31%).

    Industry observers note that the ubiquity of short-form video is one factor that seems to be making ads more palatable across social media. Since the release of DoubleVerify’s 2025 Global Insights Report, 8% more consumers have decided that social media platforms are suitable locations for ads. YouTube, at 72%, was deemed the most valid platform for those spots.

    DoubleVerify’s report shows that social media spend is paying off across multiple platforms, but marketers must still pick and choose as they allocate their ad dollars. As we saw with the Pew Research Center’s recent survey of American social media habits, usage data can vary wildly depending on demographic filters like age, gender, and household income.

    That assertion held true in the DoubleVerify report, in which TikTok ranked as the third most-used platform among 18-to-24-year-olds but didn’t crack the top five among the 65+ set. And most platforms skewed male worldwide, but 8% more female respondents use Pinterest compared to men.

    The global scope of DoubleVerify’s report adds another wrinkle to the conversation. In the Asia-Pacific region, for example, 56% of respondents said that influencer activity “somewhat to significantly” impacted purchase decisions. In North America, that statistic is only 39%. So if marketers want to ensure that their social media activity inspires action, they should deploy their budgets wisely.

    #67015. Canvas Worldwide’s Agentic Layer Helps Zillow Distinguish Real Renters From Dreamers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (868 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Canvas Worldwide’s Agentic Layer Helps Zillow Distinguish Real Renters From Dreamers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We’ve all been there: You look up a product out of sheer curiosity with no intent to actually spend money on it, and suddenly you’re inundated with ads for similar products.
    • The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.
    • Industry observers note that zillow knows that challenge well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We’ve all been there: You look up a product out of sheer curiosity with no intent to actually spend money on it, and suddenly you’re inundated with ads for similar products.

    The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.

    Industry observers note that zillow knows that challenge well. Its rental site often serves as a place for people to fantasize about their future home, even if they’re not actually looking to move.

    Sources indicate that “We are known for dreaming,” said Ravi Kandikonda, SVP of marketing for Zillow Group. But that’s not necessarily a bad thing. Welcoming the dreamers is a great way for Zillow to drive awareness of its brand and get potential future renters into its platform, Kandikonda added. From there, it’s a matter of striking a balance between building awareness and driving conversions.

    That’s where Zillow turns to its media agency partner, Canvas Worldwide.

    In September, Canvas confirmed a fresh division called ART Dept., which provides a collection of AI solutions to help brands and agencies optimize their campaign budgeting and pacing. Zillow is using ART Dept.’s AI agents to better separate the renters from the dreamers and tailor its marketing accordingly.

    The “ART” in ART Dept. stands for “AI Applied Research and Technology.” (Though, if we’re being pedantic, wouldn’t that be AART – or AIART?).

    In a recent development, quibbles about acronyms aside, Canvas’ newly introduced division offers a mix of AI optimization features that are becoming commonplace for ad agencies and marketing platforms. Though, like other agentic platforms, Canvas states its differentiation comes from how it applies those optimizations to its agentic layer.

    For example, offering a pacing dashboard is “table stakes” by now, rather than a distinguishing feature for an agency, noted Sally Lee, SVP of programmatic and ART at Canvas.

    But Canvas wanted to make its pacing dashboard “multidimensional” by connecting it with a budget source of truth and building an agentic layer on top of it, said Lee.

    The agentic layer, called Talos, determines whether a campaign is underpacing or overpacing and optimizes for better performance. Before pushing the newly optimized campaign into the platform, a member of the Canvas team reviews and approves (or denies) it.

    It has been revealed that canvas can “pick and choose from different search and behavioral categories” to optimize against, said Lee. In Zillow’s case, that might include whether a user is researching renter’s insurance or looking into moving truck rentals.

    Canvas gets those behavioral signals through its data partnerships, including its MCP connection to predictive audience targeting company Dstillery.

    Access to behavioral data has helped Zillow reach more specific audiences and be smarter about exactly where and when to target them, said Kandikonda.

    For instance, targeting multifamily renters in Seattle using a generic, off-the-shelf “multifamily apartment buildings” audience only goes so far, he noted. “I need to know when they are on a particular platform” to bid for that audience at the right moment with the right content, he added.

    Dstillery’s audience modeling predicts which websites the target audience will visit and when based on real behavioral data. And Canvas’ AI can help surface audience and behavioral overlaps that might have previously gone overlooked by its team.

    Canvas’ reliance on data-backed reasoning was a major draw for Zillow when the two first started working together in 2023, Kandikonda stated, and it continues to be a major focus of ART Dept.

    The goal behind the fresh product suite is to save media teams time figuring out what media is performing and how much to spend on different audience segments.

    Increasing ROI is crucial for any brand. But it’s particularly important within the real estate market, Kandikonda noted, as marketing dollars are constrained and the entire industry “is bouncing around the box.”.

    So, while Zillow appreciates its dreamer audience, it’s feeling the same pressure most brands are to focus on lower-funnel conversions, such as “actual movers,” Kandikonda said.

    That’s part of the reason off-the-shelf renter audiences weren’t cutting it for Zillow’s ads business, he added.

    An off-the-shelf audience may indicate people who are interested in renting more broadly, he said, but ART was able to select for people who were actively in the process of planning a move. And more precise targeting means better lower-funnel ad performance.

    The destination, not the journey.

    From Zillow’s perspective, the biggest change from using Canvas’ ART Dept. is the results, rather than the process. After all, the AI tools are used by the Canvas team, rather than by Zillow.

    Zillow just tells Canvas what outcome it wants to achieve. Canvas then translates the desired outcome into a scorecard that weights different goals and metrics within the interoperable tech infrastructure that powers the ART Dept., which is called +Suite.

    From there, Canvas’ Audience+ product (which is similar to a data management platform) connects to data partners and the Talos AI agent to build custom audiences. Finally, Talos activates and optimizes the campaign.

    The system creates an ongoing feedback loop, said Canvas’ Lee: “Build an audience, activate it, see how it’s performing against what that client cares about and identify where to make changes to drive a better outcome.”.

    Industry News: Only You Can Prevent JavaScript Security Hacks; AppLovin Eyes A Criteo Acquisition

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Adding to the myriad IT outages and cybersecurity scares of the past month, a major malware attack recently hit 178 publications and organizations that use Optimizely’s A/B testing and analytics tools.
    • The list included the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, but the problem extends well beyond those high-profile sites.
    • “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply-chain attacks, and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators,” Zach Edwards, a researcher for Infoblox and the co-founder of DecryptAds, tells Daniel Krebs of Krebs on Security.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Adding to the myriad IT outages and cybersecurity scares of the past month, a major malware attack recently hit 178 publications and organizations that use Optimizely’s A/B testing and analytics tools.

    The list included the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, but the problem extends well beyond those high-profile sites. The concern is that many operators don’t audit the tech vendors that drop JavaScript onto their pages.

    “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply-chain attacks, and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators,” Zach Edwards, a researcher for Infoblox and the co-founder of DecryptAds, tells Daniel Krebs of Krebs on Security.

    It has been revealed that the “content security policies” (or CSPs) Edwards refers to set limits on what third-party code can do on a site, including what it can load or inject. Of the 178 affected Optimizely accounts, only 24 had CSPs in place and enforced them. Those 24 didn’t spread the malware.

    Because the malware ran in the site’s JavaScript, visitors to pages without CSPs could be infected simply by loading the page – no click or scroll required.

    The main offender, btw, in terms of third-party JavaScript abusers that expose sites to hackers, is ad tech, of course. It’s not even close. Which is why, unfortunately, as Krebs notes, downloading a modern ad blocker is the best solution for consumers to protect themselves.

    The rumor mill is heating up as the year winds down.

    Recent findings suggest that criteo has been part of that chatter for a while, with private equity firms Vista Equity and Quinti Capital reportedly interested in taking it private. Criteo hasn’t exactly thrived as a public tech giant, after all.

    But it does possess an immense graph of shopper info.

    And now another contender has reportedly entered the ring. According to Reuters, AppLovin is among those in talks with Criteo.

    Significant companies can use deal talks to get an inside look at the finances and operations of smaller companies. Even if the deal doesn’t happen, they’ve still gotten a peek under the hood.

    According to recent reports, amazon, for example, was rumored to have considered Criteo once upon a time – not long before launching its own off-site retargeting. Hmm.

    In a recent development, but Criteo would be an interesting fit for AppLovin. It plugs into a wide network of retailers and web publishers – an entirely latest arena to AppLovin, which operates almost entirely in-app – and would bring a large book of business with ecommerce companies. AppLovin has remarked that it’s a priority to add advertisers to its “consumer” segment, which is primarily ecommerce.

    Criteo would offer a cheat code to get there.

    In a recent development, the rise of residential proxy services that hide bot traffic behind real human IP addresses has been a boon for ad fraud. Often, consumers aren’t even aware they’re acting as a proxy for bot traffic.

    Now, cheap consumer electronics with backdoor vulnerabilities built in can deliver billions of fraudulent ad impressions per day, according to a latest report by HUMAN Security’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team.

    The latest scheme Satori uncovered, which it dubbed BADBOX 3.0, was responsible for 40 billion fraudulent bid requests a day at its peak. It used the same residential proxy infrastructure as two other fraud rings that were uncovered by Satori in the past two years – hence the “3.0” branding.

    The infrastructure relies on cheap TV sets manufactured in China by a company called TXCZ. These TVs have backdoors in their operating systems that allow fraudsters to compromise them.

    Once they’re compromised, the TVs run video ads in the background that the TV owner cannot see. The bid requests for these ads use the TV owner’s IP address to appear as if they’re targeted to a real human. They also impersonate traffic from legitimate CTV apps.

    People who bought one of these TVs pretty much had no chance.

    “It was compromised before you plugged it in: playing video ads you could never see and quietly renting out your home internet connection to strangers,” states HUMAN’s Gavin Reid. “Neither the advertisers paying for those ads nor the people who bought the boxes had any idea.”.

    YouTube adjusts its video view counts with modeled co-viewers based on its estimate of how many people saw the screen. [The Verge].

    Netflix is the frontrunner in a bidding war over the broadcast rights for the 2030 FIFA World Cup, with experts expecting FIFA to charge up to $2 billion. [The Guardian].

    Sources indicate that taylor Swift’s unveiled return to the Country Music Awards – her first appearance since 2013 – gave Disney and ABC a chance to squeeze more ad revenue from an event that had already sold out its inventory. [Variety].

    The former editor-in-chief of gaming industry publication Game Developer explains why she recently advised Redditors not to pursue a career in journalism and shares how multiple corporate owners failed to find viable monetization models for the publications she’s worked for since 2006. [ReaderGrev].

    Industry observers note that anthropic priced its initial shares at $83 apiece after demand exceeded expectations. [WSJ].

    Recent findings suggest that former Jaguar Land Rover North America CMO Charlotte Blank joins behavioral science startup Hive Science as its first-ever chief marketing officer. [MediaPost].

    #67010. Measuring Clicks Is Making ChatGPT Ads Look Like A Bad Bet

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (846 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Measuring Clicks Is Making ChatGPT Ads Look Like A Bad Bet

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The first question marketers ask about every new advertising channel is almost always the same: Does it perform better than the last one we tested?
    • It has been revealed that it happened with social.
    • The debate around ChatGPT advertising has quickly become a comparison with Google Search.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The first question marketers ask about every new advertising channel is almost always the same: Does it perform better than the last one we tested?

    It has been revealed that it happened with social. It happened with retail media. And now it’s happening with OpenAI.

    The debate around ChatGPT advertising has quickly become a comparison with Google Search. Can it deliver lower CPAs? Does it convert as well? Is it ready to compete for performance budgets?

    According to recent reports, they’re all understandable questions. But they’re the wrong ones.

    It’s a mistake to assume conversational AI should behave like search in the first place. The customer journey is fundamentally different. If marketers continue evaluating ChatGPT using search-era metrics, there’s a real risk they’ll dismiss one of the most significant fresh advertising channels before they’ve understood how it creates value.

    Google built the world’s most successful advertising business by harvesting intent.

    It has been revealed that if a user searches for “cheap hotels in Hawaii,” Google shares a list of relevant results. The commercial intent is already there. The advertiser’s job is simply to be the most relevant answer when the purchase decision is made. But conversational AI works differently.

    Instead of typing in a few keywords, a user might go into detail and explain that they’re travelling to Hawaii for a friend’s wedding, that they’re on a tight budget but want their own room, oh, and they’d like to surf while they’re there. That’s no longer a search query; it’s a conversation. And that difference matters.

    In a recent development, rather than simply capturing existing demand, conversational AI helps users explore options and refine priorities before they buy. When the traveler eventually visits the website to book, they’ve often already used AI to compare all the alternatives and understand exactly what they’re looking for.

    The advertising opportunity is participating in how intent develops.

    One of the first things marketers notice when they begin testing conversational AI is that the acquisition metrics can look uncomfortable.

    Recent findings suggest that CPAs can appear higher than those achieved through search. For anyone used to judging performance through traditional attribution, that’s an easy reason to conclude the channel isn’t competitive.

    That was my first reaction, too.

    Recent findings suggest that if it looks like search and behaves like search, surely it should produce similar economics. But once you step back and look at the customer journey rather than the click, that conclusion becomes much harder to support.

    According to recent reports, A user spending several minutes discussing products, asking follow-up questions and refining their requirements is behaving very differently from someone typing a short keyword into Google. They’re effectively qualifying themselves before they ever reach an advertiser’s website.

    That means acquisition might cost more, but the customer arriving at the other end can also be significantly better informed and a much stronger commercial fit.

    Judging conversational AI purely on CPA risks confusing efficiency with effectiveness.

    The measurement frameworks we’ve inherited aren’t suited for where the consumer journey is going.

    For more than two decades, performance marketing has been built around clicks because clicks were observable. Attribution models rewarded whichever interaction happened closest to the conversion, giving marketers a practical way to optimize campaigns at scale.

    That made perfect sense in an internet dominated by search engines, display advertising and relatively linear customer journeys.

    According to recent reports, conversational AI changes that, because the interaction influencing a purchase often happens long before a click ever occurs. And when the eventual conversion happens later through another channel, traditional attribution naturally gives the credit elsewhere.

    That doesn’t necessarily mean the initial conversation had little value; it simply means the measurement framework wasn’t designed to capture it.

    Early evidence suggests that when marketers move beyond attribution and begin measuring incremental business outcomes instead, conversational AI looks very different from the picture painted by last-click metrics.

    AI advertising can work very effectively. But unless marketers are measuring it in a way that reflects how the channel actually influences buying decisions, it can create a colossal education gap.

    The conversation today largely centers on whether OpenAI can compete with Google.

    A far better question is whether conversational AI should be evaluated like search at all.

    Every evolution in advertising has forced marketers to rethink measurement. Social wasn’t simply another display channel. Retail media wasn’t just paid search inside a retailer’s website. CTV couldn’t be judged solely through linear TV metrics.

    Conversational AI deserves the same mindset shift.

    Google monetized search intent. Conversational AI has the potential to monetize the conversation that creates it.

    Those are fundamentally different commercial models. If marketers continue measuring one using the rules of the other, they risk underestimating not only the performance of OpenAI ads, but the role conversational AI is likely to play in the future of digital advertising.

    “Data-Driven Thinking” is written by members of the media community and contains fresh ideas on the digital revolution in media.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1030 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Meet OpenX’s Upcoming CEO, An Optimistic Realist

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Safari is cracking down on identity vendors, DSPs are going direct to publishers, Google gets to keep AdX, agents are threatening to cut out the middlemen, the walled gardens keep winning and the open web is under pressure.
    • In early November, OpenX named Robert Horler as its latest CEO, taking the reins from interim chief Joshua Metzger, who returned to his role as chief legal officer.
    • According to recent reports, horler joins at a time of upheaval for the ad industry and one of readjustment for OpenX.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Safari is cracking down on identity vendors, DSPs are going direct to publishers, Google gets to keep AdX, agents are threatening to cut out the middlemen, the walled gardens keep winning and the open web is under pressure.

    In early November, OpenX named Robert Horler as its latest CEO, taking the reins from interim chief Joshua Metzger, who returned to his role as chief legal officer.

    According to recent reports, horler joins at a time of upheaval for the ad industry and one of readjustment for OpenX. In January, the manufacturer lost John “JG” Gentry, its CEO for nearly 15 years, after a long battle with cancer.

    According to recent reports, A 30-year veteran of agencies, advertising and ad tech, Horler previously ran Dentsu Aegis Network in the US and Northern Europe, was COO of Quantcast and, most recently, led creator agency Whalar as chief exec before it was acquired by Accenture earlier this year. He’s still on the Whalar board.

    Recent findings suggest that but, given the state of the industry, how was Horler feeling roughly a week in at OpenX? Not too bad. He’s a glass-half-full kinda guy, but he’s also a pragmatist.

    “Everybody’s being disrupted,” Horler said. “You can pull the blanket over your head and say, ‘No thanks,’ or you can see an amazing amount of opportunity for companies that are agile and ambitious. I fancy our chances.”.

    Horler spoke with AdExchanger about Apple’s latest move, whether the sell side has the upper hand right now and the massive boots he has to fill.

    AdExchanger: Let’s start with the state of play. The assumption for a long time was that as the line blurred between the buy side and sell side, DSPs would come out on top. Now it feels like the sell side has the power. Is that how you see it?

    ROBERT HORLER: I’d agree, but it’s complicated. The pendulum has swung toward supply because advertisers want to get closer to the data and the publisher.

    Sources indicate that for the first time in about 30 years, the bigger agencies are pursuing divergent strategies for how they work with SSPs and DSPs. They all want more control, more orchestration and more influence over the revenue they drive, and I’d hypothesize that SSPs are well placed to deliver that.

    Also, no slight to The Trade Desk, but if the biggest cat in the jungle is having this many existential challenges, that tells you something’s going on.

    Speaking of massive cats, OpenX is suing Google, as is Magnite, PubMatic and Index Exchange. I know there’s not much you can say about OpenX’s lawsuit, if anything, but as an industry observer, what did you think of the fact that Google didn’t have to divest AdX in the federal ad tech antitrust case?

    According to recent reports, you know, it’s a shame. It’s tough for everybody who thought there would be one, but I can’t say that I’m surprised there wasn’t.

    Sources indicate that A lot of sell-side players are going buyer-direct. So is everything just everything now? Are the distinctions between buy-side and the sell-side tech no longer meaningful?

    For the people who aren’t in it, who don’t work in ad tech or programmatic advertising – and that includes some clients – the lines have always felt quite blurred. That’s not new.

    Sources indicate that there’s probably not as much difference now as there was, though. Things are converging and overlapping and people are encroaching a bit into each other’s territories as they figure out the brave upcoming agentic landscape. And, of course, there are also pressures that exist within their own businesses.

    But what will always be true is that publishers want to generate as much yield as possible and advertisers want to pay as little as possible, as long as it’s still effective, of course. So, yes, perhaps those lines are blurring a bit, but this natural tension will always exist.

    I know you’re still settling in, but how about you approaching Apple’s move to block identity vendors in iOS 27?

    This is a major question that needs to be considered, and it’s not about workarounds; it’s about understanding it. I’m sure Joel [Meyer, OpenX’s CTO] and his team are all over it. But I don’t think it’s an existential challenge or that it represents a massively different challenge to other challenges we’ve had to navigate in the past in terms of privacy, control and all those good things.

    That’s all I can say right now other than that no one here is walking around and behaving like it’s an extinction event or something.

    It has been revealed that you spent the better part of a decade on the buy side, including as the US CEO of Dentsu. What do buyers get wrong about the sell side?

    According to recent reports, I’d flip it, actually. The sell side needs to be simpler to partner with and more able to adapt, and sometimes they forget that. The sell side also underestimates how overwhelmed buyers are with choices.

    If you show up with an overly complex sell or a raft of products that you can’t explain in simple language, you’ll just sound like everyone else. Also, don’t underestimate the importance of humanity. Trust is built around people, not just technology.

    Recent findings suggest that I wanted to ask about John. He was such a lovely man, and his death was such a loss. How will you keep his legacy alive?

    Industry observers note that I never got to meet him, and I really wish I had. He was clearly beloved. When I came in for my board interview, I read the remembrance book here and it was really moving. It made me think, “If I get this job, those are big boots to fill.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the best way to honor him is to continue the mission and build a valuable organization where people enjoy coming into work. John clearly believed culture is preeminent and that it’s the people who make a great company, and I want to lead with that in mind.

    This interview has been lightly edited and condensed.
